Hera’s 1st closeup view of Didymos and Dimorphos

The European Space Agency (ESA) said this week (November 5, 2026) that its Hera mission has caught a first glimpse of its target asteroid system. The larger asteroid in this binary system is Didymos. The smaller object – considered a moonlet of Didymos — is Dimorphos. NASA’s DART mission — the world’s first planetary defense test — struck Dimorphos back in 2022.

Hera is the follow-up mission, meant to gather details on DART’s strike. The spacecraft was about 37 miles (60 km) away from Didymos when it acquired the image above. Little Dimorphos also makes an appearance in this image, from its hiding place in the larger asteroid’s shadow. Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel said:

The first thing we said was wow! This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world. This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.

ESA’s Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers added:

Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km (.6 mi) of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it might be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material.

And we have an exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.

ESA said that detailed images of both asteroids will be unveiled on November 25.

DART mission and Hera mission

In 2022, the groundbreaking DART mission struck and moved an asteroid. It was a test of Earth’s ability to defend itself from an incoming asteroid threat. Read more: When DART struck Dimorphos

ESA’s Hera launched two years later, on October 7, 2024. It’s a follow-up mission to DART. After it arrives, it’ll spend six months investigating the aftereffects from the DART impact. Hera’s main mission is to determine how effectively the impact changed the orbit of Dimorphos. It’ll also look at Dimorphos’ and Didymos’ physical structure. In other words, DART demonstrated that we can deliberately alter an asteroid’s motion. Hera is going back to investigate the details.

Why? Because if an asteroid were headed for Earth, we’d want to know as much as possible about how to knock it off course!

So far in 2026, the Hera mission has undergone a deep-space maneuver to correct its course toward its target. And in July 2026, it finished receiving an upgrade to its software. A braking maneuver on October 15 also worked to get the spacecraft to its target.

When Hera reaches the two asteroids, it’ll release two cubesats, Milani and Juventas. Milani is in charge of spectral surface observations (splitting light bounced off the asteroid into a rainbow array of colors, then analyzing that light) of both Didymos and Dimorphos. And Juventas will take the first radar soundings in the heart of an asteroid.

According to ESA — the mission planner — Hera will conduct a “crime scene investigation” at Dimorphos. But Hera will also check out both Didymos and the dusty environs unleashed by the impact.

Here are 3 mysteries that Hera will help solve

ESA shared three mysteries that Hera will help solve:

  1. Hera will measure the density and composition of Dimorphos in detail and help scientists determine whether it is a “rubble pile” loosely held together by gravity, or a solid core covered in boulders and gravel.
  2. Hera will map the crater created by DART’s impact down to 4-inch (10-cm) resolution to help scientists better understand how the surface material responded to the collision. It’s possible that there is no crater at all, but rather the impact reshaped the entire asteroid!
  3. About 15% of known asteroids are actually binary systems, but their origins remain mysterious. Hera will determine whether Dimorphos and Didymos are made from the same material, which would hint that the rapidly spinning Didymos once threw off debris into space that later formed Dimorphos.

Bottom line: The Hera mission just got its 1st closeup view of the asteroid Didymos and its little moonlet Dimorphos. Soon it will begin investigating the aftermath of the DART impact.

About the Author:

Deborah Byrd (asteroid 3505 Byrd) helps edit EarthSky.org and is a frequent host of EarthSky videos. Deborah created the EarthSky radio series in 1991 and founded EarthSky.org in 1994. Prior to that, she had worked for the University of Texas McDonald Observatory since 1976, and created and produced their Star Date radio series. She has won a galaxy of awards from the broadcasting and science communities, including having an asteroid named in her honor in 1990, a Public Service Award from the National Science Board in 2003, and the Education Prize from the American Astronomical Society in 2020. A science communicator and educator since 1976, Byrd believes in science as a force for good in the world and a vital tool for the 21st century. "Being an EarthSky editor is like hosting a big global party for cool nature-lovers," she says.
